w: obedientia passiva (Latin) — suffering obedience; Christ’s willing submission to suffering and death to pay the penalty for our sin
g: Theologians speak of Christ’s obedience in two ways. His active obedience is his perfect keeping of God’s law throughout his life (see Active Obedience of Christ).

w: status humiliationis / exaltationis (Latin) — the two states of Christ: his lowering of himself to the cross and the grave, and his raising to glory
g: Theologians describe Christ’s saving work in two “states”. His humiliation is the downward path: from the glory of heaven to birth, a lowly life, suffering, death and burial.

w: ho eschatos Adam (Greek) — the last Adam; Christ as the new head of humanity, who undoes what the first Adam did
g: Paul calls Jesus “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Adam was the first man and the head of the human race; what he did affected everyone who came from him. Jesus is a second head of a new humanity.

w: ho amnos tou theou (Greek) — the Lamb of God; Jesus as the sacrifice God provides to take away the sin of the world
g: When John the Baptist saw Jesus coming, he cried, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). In one phrase John gathered up centuries of Old Testament sacrifice and pointed it all at Jesus.

w: lytron (Greek) — ransom, the price of release; Christ’s life given as the price that sets captives free
g: A ransom is a price paid to set someone free — a captive, a prisoner of war, a slave. Jesus used this word for his own death: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

w: poena (Latin) penalty + substitutio, substitution; Christ bearing in our place the penalty our sins deserved
g: Penal substitution is the teaching that on the cross Christ took our place (substitution) and bore the punishment for our sins (penal, from the Latin for penalty).

w: peccatum originale (Latin) — original sin; the guilt and corruption that all people inherit from Adam’s first sin
g: Original sin does not mean the first sin Adam committed, but the sinful condition every human being has from the origin of their life because of Adam. It has two parts: guilt — we share in the guilt of Adam’s sin, because he represented us — and corruption — we are born with a nature bent toward sin.

w: foedus (Latin) — covenant; Adam and Christ as covenant representatives whose actions count for those they represent
g: “Federal” comes from the Latin foedus, covenant. Federal headship is the teaching that God deals with humanity through two covenant heads, or representatives: Adam and Christ.

w: gratia irresistibilis (Latin) — effective grace; the Holy Spirit’s work that infallibly brings God’s chosen people to faith
g: Irresistible grace (sometimes called effectual grace) is the teaching that when God sets out to save someone, his grace accomplishes what he intends. The Holy Spirit so works in a sinner’s heart that they come to Christ willingly.

w: epistrophē (Greek) / shuv (Hebrew) — turning; the sinner’s turning from sin to God in repentance and faith
g: Conversion is turning — turning away from sin and turning to God in Christ. The Hebrew shuv and the Greek epistrephō both mean to turn around. The Thessalonians “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

w: plērophoria (Greek) — full assurance, certainty; a believer’s confident knowledge that they belong to Christ
g: Assurance is a Christian’s confidence that they truly belong to Christ and will be saved. It is possible to be saved and not feel sure, and it is possible to feel sure and not be saved.

w: servum arbitrium (Latin) — the bound will; the fallen human will, which cannot by itself choose God
g: The bondage of the will is the teaching that since the fall, the human will is not free to choose God by its own power. We are free to choose what we want, but what we want, by nature, is not God.

w: torah (Hebrew) / nomos (Greek) — instruction, law; God’s revealed will for human life, summed up in the Ten Commandments
g: God’s law is his revealed will for how we should live. The Hebrew torah means instruction or teaching; it can refer to the Ten Commandments, the books of Moses, or the whole Old Testament.

w: lex et evangelium (Latin) — law and gospel; the distinction between God’s commands and God’s promise of salvation in Christ
g: Law and gospel are two different kinds of word God speaks. The law tells us what we must do: “Do this, and you will live” (Luke 10:28). The gospel tells us what God has done in Christ: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31).

w: nomism — a reliance on law-keeping; trying to earn God’s favour, or to add human rules to his word
g: Legalism is a distortion of God’s law. It takes two main forms. The first is trying to earn God’s favour or salvation by keeping rules. The second is adding human rules to God’s word and treating them as if they were his commands.

w: anti (against) + nomos (law) — lawlessness; the error that because we are saved by grace, God’s law has no claim on the believer
g: Antinomianism means “against the law”. It is the error of thinking that because Christians are saved by grace and not by works, God’s moral law no longer applies to them.

w: mortificatio (Latin) — putting to death; the believer’s Spirit-empowered fight to kill sin
g: Mortification means putting sin to death. It comes from the Latin mors, death. Paul writes, “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13), and “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5).

w: syneidēsis (Greek) — conscience; the inner sense of right and wrong that accuses or excuses us before God
g: Conscience is the inner sense, given by God, that judges our actions and thoughts as right or wrong. It accuses us when we do wrong and approves when we do right.

w: peirasmos (Greek) — testing, trial, temptation; an enticement to sin, or a trial that tests faith
g: The Greek word peirasmos can mean either a test (a trial God sends to strengthen faith) or a temptation (an enticement to sin). The same situation can be both: God tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and Satan tempted Job through the same losses God permitted.

w: enoikeō (Greek) — to dwell in; the Holy Spirit living within every believer
g: The indwelling of the Spirit means that the Holy Spirit lives within every Christian. Not merely beside us or occasionally visiting, but making his home in us. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

w: phōtismos (Greek) — enlightening; the Holy Spirit’s work of opening our minds to understand and receive the truth of Scripture
g: Illumination is the work of the Holy Spirit in which he opens our minds and hearts to understand, believe and love the truth of God’s word. Inspiration is the Spirit’s work in the writers of Scripture; illumination is his work in its readers.

w: karpos tou pneumatos (Greek) — fruit of the Spirit; the Christlike character the Holy Spirit grows in every believer
g: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

w: vocatio (Latin) — calling; God’s call to serve him and our neighbour in the ordinary places of life
g: Vocation means “calling”. The medieval church used it mainly for priests, monks and nuns, who were thought to have a higher, spiritual calling. The Reformers recovered the biblical teaching that every Christian has a calling from God — not only to salvation, but to serve him in ordinary life: as a parent, worker, neighbour and citizen.

w: charismata (Greek) — gifts of grace; abilities given by the Holy Spirit to each believer for building up the church
g: Spiritual gifts are abilities the Holy Spirit gives to believers so that they can serve others and build up the church. The Greek word charismata comes from charis, grace: they are gifts of grace, not rewards for spiritual achievement.

w: sacramentum (Latin) — a sacred sign; a visible sign and seal of God’s promise, instituted by Christ
g: A sacrament is a holy sign and seal of God’s covenant promises, given by Christ to his church. Augustine called it “a visible word”. In a sacrament, God takes ordinary things — water, bread, wine — and uses them to show and confirm the gospel to our senses.

w: media gratiae (Latin) — means of grace; the ordinary channels God uses to give and strengthen faith: the word, the sacraments and prayer
g: The means of grace are the ordinary ways God uses to bring people to faith and to make them grow. The Shorter Catechism names them: “the outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption are, his ordinances, especially the word, sacraments, and prayer” (Q. 88).

w: presbyteros (Greek) / episkopos (Greek) — elder, overseer; a man called to shepherd and govern a local church
g: Elders are the spiritual leaders of a local church. The New Testament uses several words for the same office: presbyteros (elder, emphasising maturity), episkopos (overseer or bishop, emphasising oversight) and poimēn (shepherd or pastor, emphasising care).

w: diakonos (Greek) — servant, minister; an officer of the church who leads in practical service and mercy
g: The Greek word diakonos simply means servant. Jesus used it of himself: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). In the New Testament it also names a specific church office: deacons, who lead the church’s practical ministry, especially care for the poor and needy.

w: disciplina ecclesiastica (Latin) — church discipline; the church’s loving correction of members who persist in serious sin, for their restoration
g: Church discipline is the church’s responsibility to correct its members who fall into serious, unrepentant sin, with the aim of bringing them back. It is like a family’s discipline of its children — not punishment for its own sake, but love that will not let someone walk away from God without a fight.

w: kleides tēs basileias (Greek) — the keys of the kingdom; the authority Christ gives his church to open and shut the kingdom through preaching and discipline
g: Jesus told Peter, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

w: ecclesia visibilis / invisibilis (Latin) — the church as it appears on earth, and the church as God sees it: all the elect in every age
g: Reformed theology speaks of the church in two ways. The invisible church is the whole company of God’s chosen people — all who truly belong to Christ, in every age and place, known fully only to God.

w: notae ecclesiae (Latin) — the marks of the church; the signs by which a true church can be recognised
g: The marks of the church are the signs by which you can recognise a true church. In the Reformation, people needed to know: if Rome had departed from the gospel, where was the true church to be found?

w: principle that worship is regulated by Scripture; God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has commanded in his word
g: The regulative principle of worship says that God must be worshipped only in the ways he has appointed in Scripture. Whatever God commands for worship, we do; what he does not command, we do not add.

w: kyriakē hēmera (Greek) — the Lord’s Day; Sunday, the first day of the week, set apart for worship and rest in honour of Christ’s resurrection
g: The Lord’s Day is Sunday, the first day of the week, which Christians set apart for worship and rest. John was “in the Spirit on the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10).

w: pentēkostē (Greek) — fiftieth; the Jewish harvest festival fifty days after Passover, when the Holy Spirit was poured out on the church
g: Pentecost means “fiftieth”. It was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, held fifty days after Passover, when Israel gave thanks for the first fruits of the wheat harvest (Leviticus 23:15–21).

w: kohen (Hebrew) / hiereus (Greek) — priest; one who represents people before God and offers sacrifices on their behalf
g: A priest stands between God and people. He represents the people before God, offers sacrifices for their sins, prays for them and blesses them in God’s name. “For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Hebrews 5:1).

w: mishkan (Hebrew) — dwelling place; the portable tent-sanctuary where God dwelt among Israel in the wilderness
g: The tabernacle was the portable sanctuary Israel built in the wilderness at God’s command. The Hebrew word mishkan means “dwelling place”. God said, “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (Exodus 25:8).

w: pesach (Hebrew) — passing over; the feast remembering the night God spared Israel’s firstborn and brought them out of Egypt
g: Passover is the feast that remembers the night God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. God sent a final plague: the death of every firstborn. But each Israelite family killed a lamb without blemish and put its blood on the doorposts.

w: she’ar (Hebrew) / leimma (Greek) — what remains; the faithful few whom God preserves for himself in times of widespread unbelief
g: The remnant is the small group of faithful people whom God preserves when most of his people turn away. The word means “what is left over”. Throughout the Bible, when judgment falls, God always keeps a remnant for himself, so that his promises do not fail.

w: typos (Greek) — pattern, model, type; the way people, events and institutions in the Old Testament foreshadow Christ and his salvation
g: Typology is the study of “types”: real people, events and institutions in the Old Testament that God designed to foreshadow Christ and the salvation he brings. The Greek word typos means a pattern or imprint.

w: geenna (Greek) — Gehenna, hell; the place of final, conscious punishment for those who die without Christ
g: Hell is the place of God’s final judgment on unrepentant sinners. The New Testament word Gehenna comes from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had once been sacrificed to idols and which became a symbol of judgment (Jeremiah 7:31–32).

w: krisis (Greek) — judgment; the day when Christ will judge all people, living and dead, and every secret will be revealed
g: The final judgment is the day at the end of history when Jesus Christ will judge all people. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

w: mille anni (Latin) — a thousand years; the reign of Christ described in Revelation 20, understood in different ways by Christians
g: “Millennium” means a thousand years. It comes from Revelation 20:1–6, where Satan is bound for a thousand years and the saints “came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (Revelation 20:4).

w: kainos ouranos kai gē (Greek) — a new heaven and a new earth; the renewed creation where God will dwell with his people for ever
g: The final hope of Scripture is not that we escape the world, but that God will make it new. “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away” (Revelation 21:1).

w: en Christō (Greek) — union with Christ; the most fundamental description of the believer's identity
g: "In Christ" is Paul's favourite phrase. He uses it, or its equivalents ("in him," "in the Lord"), over 160 times. It is not a piece of religious decoration. It is the most fundamental statement that can be made about a Christian — more foundational than your behaviour, your feelings, your progress, your failures.
